title: Casimir force in a water nanolayer confined by graphene sheets
abstract: Casimir forces, arising from quantum and thermal fluctuations, depend strongly on the electromagnetic susceptibilities of the interacting materials. Here, we theoretically investigate the Casimir force between two graphene sheets separated by a nanometer-thin layer of liquid water. We find that, at thicknesses up to 3.4 nm, the confinement reduces the Casimir force by up to 26 % compared to the bulk case. At larger thicknesses, the bulk model underestimates the Casimir force by up to 42 % due to the interface effect. This effect does not decrease monotonically as a function of the layer thickness: it increases up to a maximum at 70 nm and it slowly declines to the bulk limit only at 2 microns. We separately assess the effect of nanoscale confinement on the electronic response of graphene, which has no effect on the Casimir force.
summary: This work calculates the Casimir force between graphene sheets separated by a nanolayer of water, finding that the confinement significantly alters the force compared to bulk predictions. The deviation is attributed to both geometric confinement and surface interface effects, which are modeled using anisotropic dielectric functions. This research is vital for understanding quantum vacuum forces in liquid-graphene nano-devices.
main_problem: The paper theoretically investigates how the presence of a nanolayer of liquid water confined between two graphene sheets modifies the Casimir force between the sheets.
main_result: Confinement reduces the Casimir force by up to 26% at small thicknesses, and the bulk model significantly underestimates the force at larger separations due to interface effects, which exhibit non-monotonic behavior.
method: The Casimir force is calculated using the Lifshitz formula, requiring the solution of Maxwell's equations via the transfer matrix method for an anisotropic gap.
model_or_system: The system consists of two graphene sheets sandwiching an anisotropic water nanolayer. The water permittivity is modeled as thickness-dependent, distinguishing between confinement and interface effects.
key_observables: Casimir force ($\Pi_{	ext{Cas}}(a)$) and Casimir free energy ($	ext{E}_{	ext{Cas}}(a)$).
important_parameters: Water gap thickness ($a$), temperature ($T=300$ K), and the anisotropic dielectric tensor components ($\epsilon_{\parallel}, \epsilon_{\perp}$).
main_assumptions: The water layer is modeled as an anisotropic 3D bulk medium, and the graphene sheets are treated as 2D using the local Kubo model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of the confined system and compare the calculated Casimir pressure under confinement versus the bulk model predictions, highlighting the magnitude of the interface effect.
paper_structure: The analysis proceeds by deriving the force using the Lifshitz formula, modeling the anisotropic permittivity of the confined water using effective medium approximations, and then comparing the results to the bulk limit to quantify confinement and interface effects.
why_interesting: The study provides quantitative predictions for how nanoscale liquid structure (water) modifies fundamental quantum vacuum forces (Casimir), which is crucial for understanding quantum electrodynamics in confined geometries.
